Learning Objectives
Discuss the epidemiology of, etiology of, and risk factors for slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
Perform an appropriate workup for patients in whom slipped capital femoral epiphysis is
suspected.
Review the surgical management of stable and unstable slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
Describe the sequelae of slipped capital femoral epiphysis, particularly femoroacetabular
impingement, and options for management.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is a disorder of the skeletally immature hip in which
the femoral neck (metaphysis) displaces anteriorly and superiorly relative to the proximal

Displacement occurs through the proliferative and hypertrophic zones of the proximal femoral

The physis in SCFE is abnormally widened and organized in an irregular pattern.
Uncommonly, the femoral neck displaces posteriorly or medially relative to the femoral
epiphysis (valgus SCFE).
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
SCFE occurs if the proximal femoral metaphysis displaces (anteriorly and superiorly)
relative to the proximal femoral epiphysis through the proliferative and hypertrophic
zones of an open proximal femoral physis.
Epidemiology
SCFE is the most common disorder of the hip in adolescents.
Males are more commonly affected than females (2:1 ratio). The cumulative risk in males is 1
per 1,000 to 2,000 individuals; the risk in females is 1 per 2,000 to 3,000 individuals.
SCFE most commonly occurs during periods of rapid growth (age 10 to 14 years). Mean age is
12 years in boys and 11.2 years in girls.
Unilateral involvement is more common (80%) than bilateral involvement at the time of
presentation. Ultimately, the hips are involved bilaterally in 10% to 60% of patients
(approximately 25%).
SCFE more commonly occurs in Hispanic, Polynesian, and African American populations but
may be more of a reflection of body mass index in these racial and ethnic groups1 (Resource
1).


Epidemiology
SCFE is the most common disorder of the hip in adolescents, occurring in 1 per 2,000
individuals and more commonly in males. The most common age is 10 to 14 years;
however, SCFE may occur in patients as young as 6 years or as old as 16 years who have
open physes, especially those with endocrine disorders or who are undergoing growth
hormone treatment or other interventions.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
An open proximal femoral physis is a prerequisite for SCFE.
Changes in the inclination and anatomy of the physis during rapid growth and increased load
(obesity) or weakened physis (endocrine disorder, trisomy 21, growth hormone treatment)
results in SCFE.
Results in a three-dimensional deformity of the proximal femur
May be associated with a deep (pincer, protrusio) or retroverted acetabulum
A modified Oxford bone score of 16, 17, or 18 at the time of initial, unilateral SCFE is
associated with a 96% predictive value for contralateral slip. Alternatively, an open triradiate is
adequate as a surrogate for those scores2 (Resource 2).
Anatomy and Biomechanics

Anatomy and Biomechanics
SCFE requires an open proximal femoral physis and is associated with rapid growth and
a weakened physis. The deformity is present in all three planes. A modified Oxford bone
score or an open triradiate should prompt consideration of prophylactic fixation of the
uninvolved physis because of its high predictive value and the risk of contralateral slip
(as high as 60% in some studies; approximately 25% overall).

Injury from SCFE or iatrogenic injury may result in osteonecrosis.
Decompression of the intra-articular hematoma in patients with unstable SCFE has been
associated with decreased osteonecrosis and is thought to occur via relief of tamponade of the
MFCA.
The medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA) is the primary blood supply to the femoral
epiphysis3,4 (Resource 3; Figure 1).

supply, which is from the posterosuperior lateral epiphyseal vessels that originate from the

Vascular Anatomy
The MFCA provides direct vascular supply to the proximal femoral epiphysis and may be
directly injured by the slip, tamponade from hematoma, or iatrogenic injury.
Decompression of intra-articular hematoma in patients with unstable SCFE at the time of
in situ epiphysiodesis is recommended based on the available evidence.
Nerves
The obturator nerve may be a source of referred hip pain to the knee.
Knee pain in a child should prompt evaluation of the hip. Focus on the knee alone may lead to
unnecessary workup or management of the knee and delayed diagnosis of SCFE.
High index of suspicion for hip pathology in patients with obesity or those with
endocrinopathies, trisomy 21, or other risk factors if knee pain is present
Nerves

Nerves
Knee pain secondary to referred hip pain via the obturator nerve in pediatric and
adolescent patients, especially those at risk for SCFE, should prompt evaluation of the
hip via AP pelvis and frog-leg lateral radiographs because of the risk of delayed diagnosis
of SCFE.
Etiology
The precise etiology of SCFE is unknown but likely multifactorial.
No established genetic cause
More than 50% of cases are in patients with a weight higher than the 95th percentile. Mean
body mass index is 25 to 30 kg/m2.1

In general, SCFE is thought to result from an insufficient mechanical ability of the proximal
femoral physis to resist loading. This usually results from a combination of abnormally high
loads across an abnormally weak physis.5
Risk Factors
Conditions that weaken the physis include endocrinopathies, such as hypothyroidism,
panhypopituitarism, growth hormone abnormalities, hypogonadism, and hyper-or
hypoparathyroidism; systemic diseases, such as renal osteodystrophy, hypertension, or
hyperlipidemia; weight lower than the 10th or greater than the 90the percentiles; trisomy 21;
and prior radiation therapy to the proximal femur.5
Mechanical factors that may increase the load across the physis are associated with SCFE,
including obesity, relative or absolute femoral and acetabular retroversion, a decreased
femoral neck-shaft angle, and increased physeal obliquity, posterior epiphyseal tilt (>10°).1
Obesity may be a modifiable risk factor. The persistence of obesity after SCFE is associated
with an odds ratio of 3.5 for additional slip progression whereas weight loss is protective.1,6
Risk Factors

Risk Factors
Endocrinopathies, trisomy 21, prior radiation therapy, systemic diseases, mechanical
factors, obesity, retroversion, neck-shaft angle, physeal obliquity, and posterior
epiphyseal tilt, are risk factors for SCFE. Weight loss is protective.
Natural History
Patients present with hip or knee (referred) pain with or without ambulation.
Patents may be unable to bear weight, which is almost universally preceded by symptoms for
days to months.
Worsening pain over time versus an acute-on-chronic event
Limp
Loss of hip range of motion (ROM; especially internal rotation and flexion)

Hip or knee pain, a limp, an external foot progression angle, and obligate external
rotation in patients with an open proximal femoral physis is considered SCFE until
proven otherwise. Surgeons must closely examine and evaluate the contralateral hip.
Classification
The weight-bearing, or Loder, classification is the most widely used classification system. It
defines SCFE as stable or unstable based on a patient’s functional stability, which is
determined by ability to bear weight5 (Table 1; Resource 4).
Most cases of SCFE are stable slips (>90%).
SCFE is stable if the patient can bear weight on the involved extremity (with or without
crutches).
SCFE is unstable if the patient cannot bear weight on the involved extremity.

Classification

Classification
The value of this stability classification system is its ability to predict osteonecrosis. In a
study, the risk of osteonecrosis in unstable hips was 47% compared with that in stable
hips, which was zero7 (Resource 5).
Unstable slips result in osteonecrosis more often (4.7% to 58%) than stable slips (zero to
1.4%).

The Loder classification of functional stability is associated with poor sensitivity (39%)
and moderate specificity (76%) compared with physeal stability assessed
intraoperatively; therefore, a classification system that reflects the risk of osteonecrosis
and physeal stability is necessary8 (Resource 6). 
The traditional classification system was based on duration of symptoms; however, it has
largely been replaced by the stability classification system because of its better
prognostic value with regard to osteonecrosis. The traditional classification included the
following categories:
Chronic SCFE: symptoms have been present for more than 3 weeks
Acute SCFE: symptoms have been present for less than 3 weeks
Acute-on-chronic SCFE: acute exacerbation of symptoms follows a prodrome of
at least 3 weeks2
Radiographic Classification System

Radiographic Classification System
SCFE is graded according to the percentage of epiphyseal displacement relative to the
metaphyseal width of the femoral neck on AP or lateral radiographs. The grades are mild
(<33%), moderate (33% to 50%), and severe (>50%).
The Southwick angle (femoral epiphyseal-metaphyseal angle) is the angle formed by the
proximal femoral physis and the femoral shaft on lateral radiographs. SCFE also may be
graded based on the difference in the Southwick angle between the involved and
uninvolved hip, with respective grades of mild (<30° difference), moderate (30° to 50°
difference), or severe (>50° difference)9,10 (Figure 3).

femoral epiphysis. A line is drawn parallel to the physis, and a second line is drawn

Currently, SCFE is classified using the Loder classification system. Patients who are able
to bear weight on the affected extremity have stable SCFE. Inability to bear weight is
classified as unstable SCFE. The Loder classification system is predictive of risk of
osteonecrosis but is poorly sensitive and moderately specific with regard to actual
physeal stability. Classification of the duration of symptoms, although useful for the
clinician in determining the onset of SCFE, is not widely used or currently accepted. Mild
(<30° difference), moderate (30° to 50° difference) and severe (>50° difference) SCFE are
classified using the Southwick angle or amount of deformity compared with the
uninvolved hip. Multiple studies have reported that femoroacetabular impingement
(FAI), deterioration, and early osteoarthritis are observed after even mild slips.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical presentation

SCFE is most common in children aged 10 to 16 years.
In boys, age at presentation ranges from 12 to 16 years (mean age, 13.5 years).
In girls, age at presentation ranges from 10 to 14 years (mean age, 11.5 years).
Children with SCFE commonly have a limp and pain localized to the groin, hip, thigh, or knee
(obturator nerve).
Symptoms may be present for weeks to months before a diagnosis is made.
Patient History
Immediate-to-months-long complaints of stable or worsening hip/groin/knee pain, altered gait,
difficulty tying shoes, decreased activity, possible acute injury/exacerbation overlying chronic
course, multiple prior evaluations without plain radiographs (especially frog-lateral/cross-table
lateral views), knee surgery
Endocrine abnormalities, trisomy 21, radiation treatment, kidney disease
Physical Examination
Common physical examination findings include an abnormal gait (antalgic and/or
Trendelenburg), decreased ROM (particularly, decreased hip flexion and decreased internal
rotation), and mild limb-length discrepancy.
Assessment of hip ROM may reveal obligate external rotation (external rotation of the hip as
the hip is brought into flexion).
The foot and knee progression angles usually are externally rotated.
Physical Examination

Physical Examination
Antalgic gait or a limp, decreased hip flexion and internal rotation, mild limb-length
discrepancy, obligate external rotation, and external foot and knee progression angles
are common physical examination findings. A recent or prolonged duration of symptoms
may be reported. Patients may describe altered gait; difficulty sitting or tying shoes;
possible injury; multiple prior evaluations or holistic treatment without appropriate
radiographs; or underlying endocrine, chromosomal, or renal disease. Radiation
exposure also may be a risk factor. SCFE more commonly occurs in boys aged 10 to 16

Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standard AP and frog-lateral radiographs of the pelvis are recommended. Both hips should be
visualized. For patients who cannot be positioned for a frog-lateral radiograph (unstable SCFE),
alternate lateral views (eg, cross-table, Dunn lateral views) may be warranted.
In a normal hip, the Klein line, a line tangential to the superior border of the femoral neck on
an AP view, intersects the proximal femoral epiphysis. In a hip with SCFE, the Klein line may
fail to intersect the proximal femoral epiphysis or will be asymmetric between the two hips5
(Figure 4).
Lateral radiographs are more sensitive than other radiographic views in detecting SCFE.5
Other radiographic findings of SCFE include a widened, blurred physis and the metaphyseal
blanch sign, in which the posteriorly displaced epiphysis is superimposed on the femoral
neck on an AP view.

Imaging Studies

Imaging Studies
The preferred diagnostic imaging study is a frog-lateral radiograph, which allows for
assessment of the Klein line. An AP pelvis radiograph should be obtained at the same
time. In patients with an unstable slip, a Dunn or cross-table lateral radiograph may be
obtained to prevent additional slip. Additional findings observed on plain radiographs
include a widened, blurred physis with a metaphyseal blanch sign.
Computed Tomography
Evaluation of three-dimensional anatomy for preoperative planning in deformity correction for
chronic SCFE 
Currently, CT is not indicated for the initial diagnosis of SCFE.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may be useful for identifying a pre-slip in a symptomatic patient with normal radiographs.
An abnormally widened physis with surrounding edematous changes observed on MRI is
suggestive of such a hip.
Assess vascularity after in situ fixation or a modified Dunn procedure for the management of
unstable SCFE.

Laboratory Workup
Thyroid-stimulating hormone level, free thyroxine level
Consider additional laboratory studies and an endocrine consultation for patients younger
than 10 years or older than 16 years with a weight for height less than the 10th or greater than
the 90th percentile.
Laboratory Workup

Laboratory Workup
Thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine levels may be routinely obtained. In
addition, patients younger than 10 years or older than 16 years who have a weight for
height less than the 10th or greater than the 90th percentile should undergo endocrine
consultation, and prophylactic in situ fixation of the contralateral hip should be
considered.
Pathology
The pathology of SCFE is inherently related to an abnormal, unhealthy physis. Weakness in the
physis occurs in the hypertrophic zone and causes classic radiographic signs, such as
metaphyseal widening and irregularity. 
SCFE occurs in the hypertrophic zone of the proximal femoral physis.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis of SCFE depends on the clinical suspicion (altered gait, inability to bear weight
comfortably, knee pain, externally rotated foot progression angle, obligate external rotation on

increased posterior epiphyseal tilt, evaluation of the Southwick angle (mild/moderate/severe).
Differential Diagnosis
SCFE should be considered in the differential diagnosis for any pain about the hip and knee in
patients with open proximal femoral physes. A high index of suspicion is necessary because
SCFE often is missed. The rate of missed or delayed diagnosis of SCFE has not changed in the
past several decades11 (Resource 7).
Differential Diagnosis

Differential Diagnosis
Diagnosis depends on maintaining a high index of clinical suspicion for SCFE in patients
with open proximal physes. A limp, knee pain, external foot progression, obligate
external rotation, and disruption of the Klein line on a lateral radiograph are common
findings at diagnosis. Despite education, missed or delayed diagnosis of SCFE has
remained constant, and the duration of symptoms is directly correlated with the severity
of SCFE and complications.
Surgical Management
The goal of management is to prevent progression of the slip. SCFE should be managed
surgically as soon as it is recognized.
Stable SCFE—In situ screw fixation is the preferred initial treatment option5 (Figure 5).
Unstable SCFE—Management is controversial.
The timing of management is a subject of debate (emergent versus urgent [within 24 hours]
versus after 7 days).
Decompression of intracapsular hematoma in patients with SCFE via a capsulotomy (open or
percutaneous) may be recommended to decrease the risk of osteonecrosis.
Some tertiary care centers have shifted toward open reduction via a Smith-Petersen
approach (Parsch procedure) or via a surgical hip dislocation approach (modified Dunn

Forceful manipulation is never indicated because it is associated with an increased risk of
complications, including osteonecrosis.
Intracranial pressure or Doppler monitoring also has been used intraoperatively at certain
tertiary care centers during the management of unstable SCFE and during the modified Dunn
procedure to assess blood flow to the femoral epiphysis.
Technical points of in situ screw fixation
Large (≥6.5 mm), fully-threaded, cannulated screw systems are preferred.
A single-screw construct typically is adequate for stable SCFE. For unstable SCFE, two screws
may be considered for added stability.
The screws are started on the anterolateral femoral neck to allow them to be targeted to the
center position of the femoral head and perpendicular to the physis.
The screw starting point should be lateral to the intertrochanteric line to minimize the risk of
the screw head impinging on the acetabular rim.
Management of residual deformity
Moderate to severe posteroinferior displacement of the epiphysis relative to the metaphysis
may result in substantial proximal femoral deformities, particularly decreased femoral head-
neck offset, excessive retroversion of the femoral head, and metaphyseal prominence. These
deformities may lead to FAI and pain, stiffness, and premature osteoarthritis of the hip, even
at early follow-up.
Moderate to severe SCFE deformities can be corrected to relieve pain and improve function.
Hip arthroscopy can be performed to improve head-neck offset and manage intra-articular
pathology.
Osteotomy of the proximal femur can be performed at the subcapital, femoral neck, or
intertrochanteric (Southwick, Imhäuser) level in combination with surgical hip dislocation.
Osteotomy at the subcapital level or the level of the femoral neck may provide the greatest
correction but may be associated with higher rates of complications.
Surgical dislocation of the hip with concomitant osteoplasty and/or modified Dunn
osteotomy (deformity correction through the physis) has been safely adopted at select
centers with physicians who have considerable training and experience with this technique.


Surgical Management
The current standard of care for stable and unstable SCFE is in situ screw epiphysiodesis.
The goal of management is to prevent additional slip, increasing deformity, and
increasing risk of osteonecrosis. Timing of management is controversial. Decompression
of intracapsular hematoma is recommended in patients with unstable SCFE to decrease
the risk of osteonecrosis. Although so-called serendipitous reduction is acceptable,
closed forceful reduction of the slip is contraindicated. Initial management of unstable

SCFE at tertiary centers may include the Ledbetter, Parsch, or modified Dunn techniques.
Femoral head perfusion may be monitored via Doppler or intracranial pressure probes
to decrease the rate of osteonecrosis during these realignment procedures.
Stable SCFE may be managed via a single, fully threaded center-center screw placed
perpendicular to the physis of the capital epiphysis. The addition of a second screw of
similar size or the use of two smaller screws often is recommended in patients with
unstable SCFE. Studies recommend a minimum of four threads within the epiphysis.
Residual deformity of the proximal femur is common in patients with SCFE, may result in
symptomatic FAI or pain, and lead to premature osteoarthritis. Open and arthroscopic
techniques, such as osteoplasty, flexion-internal rotation intertrochanteric osteotomy, or
a delayed modified Dunn procedure, may improve symptoms and restore a more
functional range of motion. For each patient and family, complications related to
osteonecrosis, compliance with postoperative restrictions, and additional risks must be
weighed against potential advantages; therefore, a shared decision-making process is
recommended when considering management.
Indications
Stabilization of SCFE is indicated to prevent additional progression.
Indications for prophylactic fixation of the contralateral hip include open triradiate cartilage; a
modified Oxford bone score of 16, 17, or 18; age younger than 10 years for girls and younger
than 12 years for boys; and risk factors, such as endocrinopathies, trisomy 21, renal
osteodystrophy, and history of radiation therapy. If prophylactic fixation is not performed, the
contralateral hip should be monitored via radiographs every 6 months.
Indications

Indications
In situ epiphysiodesis of SCFE is the standard of care. Surgeons should discuss the risk of
contralateral slip (25% to 60% reported incidence) using the modified Oxford bone score.

Contraindications
Stabilization of SCFE is indicated to prevent additional progression.
Management of chronic/healed SCFE via surgical hip dislocation with modified Dunn or
proximal femur osteotomy is not indicated in hips with end-stage osteoarthritis.
Contraindications

Contraindications
In situ epiphysiodesis of SCFE is indicated in all patients. End-stage osteoarthritis is a
contraindication to surgical preservation of prior SCFE.
Techniques/Procedures
In situ fixation/pinning
Assess slip deformity and trajectory of the screw from the anterior neck to the center of the
epiphysis preoperatively.
6.5 mm or larger fully threaded screw(s) for easier fixation and removal
Two screws for unstable SCFE
Fracture table
Supine position
No traction is applied while positioning the patient to avoid injury to the retinacular vessels.
Serendipitous reduction may occur with gentle positioning.
Fluoroscopy from the contralateral side or between the legs for imaging; confirm imaging
before draping.
Flat Jackson table
Supine position

Lateral positioning allows large thigh tissue to fall away from insertion site for the guidewire.
Decompression of intracapsular hematoma via capsulotomy is recommended for unstable
SCFE. Relatively urgent stabilization has been recommended to prevent additional slip and
limit the risk of osteonecrosis; however, studies have reported a high incidence of
osteonecrosis in patients with unstable SCFE managed between 24 hours and 7 days, with
lower rates reported after 7 days or before 24 hours (Resource 8).

Techniques/Procedures
In situ epiphysiodesis of SCFE with the use of 6.5 mm or larger fully threaded cannulated
screws may be performed supine on a flat Jackson table or a fracture table. Visualization
of screw placement on lateral and AP views is necessary for optimal placement.
Serendipitous (positional) reduction is acceptable; however, traction or forced reduction
currently is not recommended, especially in patients with an unstable slip because of
concerns for disruption of the retinacular vasculature. Optimal timing of management of
unstable slips is controversial. Capsular decompression of intra-articular hematoma in
patients with unstable SCFE is recommended at the time of in situ epiphysiodesis.
Postoperative Management—Stable Versus Unstable
Weight bearing usually is protected for a minimum of 6 weeks after fixation in patients with
unstable SCFE.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Screws may be too long (ensure appropriate intraoperative imaging to prevent intra-articular
penetration), using the approach-withdraw method on live fluoroscopy. he screw heads should
not penetrate beyond the subchondral bone on any view. Failure to adhere to this technique
may result in chondrolysis.


Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Surgeons should use fully threaded screws that are 6.5 mm or larger in size. Surgeons
should avoid overpenetration of the screw heads in all patients with SCFE. Forceful
reduction should not be performed, and traction should not be applied. Surgeons
should use two screws for epiphysiodesis and perform capsular decompression in
patients with unstable SCFE.
Complications

Complications
Complications include screw failure and progression of SCFE, the need for revision with
the use of a longer screw in younger patients because of growth, chondrolysis because
of screw penetration, osteonecrosis or failure to recognize penetration at the time of
surgery, pain secondary to FAI, fracture because of placement of the screw at the lateral
cortex or in the subtrochanteric area of the femur, effusion, hemarthrosis, and concern
for deep vein thrombosis at maturity with management of chronic deformity.
Progressive SCFE
May be prevented by the addition of a second screw during in situ fixation of stable SCFE; the
addition of a second screw is recommended for unstable SCFE to prevent failed fixation.
Studies recommend placement of four threads on either side of the physis and a 6.5-mm or
larger fully-threaded screw in a center-center technique to prevent additional slip. SCFE

Young patients may grow off the screw and require revision or advancement of a purposefully

Chondrolysis
Typically caused by perforation of the osteochondral surface by the tip of the screw.
Necessitates removal and replacement. Ensure the length of the screws is appropriate on
AP/lateral fluoroscopic images as well as approach-withdrawal technique. May be prevented if
recognized and corrected.
Osteonecrosis
Approximately 25% risk in patients with unstable SCFE, less than 5% risk in patients with stable
SCFE. Hardware placement in the posterosuperior femoral neck may disrupt the MFCA, leading
to osteonecrosis. End-stage osteoarthritis secondary to osteonecrosis is more commonly
managed via total hip arthroplasty than via arthrodesis.
Pain
Usually because of FAI from metaphyseal prominence and epiphyseal retroversion. Managed
via cam resection, Dunn procedure, or proximal femoral flexion-internal rotation osteotomy
(Southwick/Imhäuser). Loss of hip ROM (internal rotation and flexion) and abductor weakness
are possible.
Fracture
Can occur at the subtrochanteric portion of the femur, usually secondary to screw entry;
minimize this risk by minimizing the number of starting point attempts with a guidewire and
by starting screws proximal to the lesser trochanter.
Effusion
May be present in patients with chronic FAI or as a hemarthrosis in patients with unstable
SCFE (decompression at the time of in situ fixation of unstable SCFE is recommended as a best
practice).

Deep Vein Thrombosis/Venous Thromboembolism
Rare; however, routine anticoagulation is not recommended for in situ fixation. Prophylaxis
varies and is not standardized after management of chronic SCFE/FAI. Patients nearing skeletal
maturity or who have a body mass index greater than 30 kg/m2 may be at higher risk;
recommend after institutional venous thromboembolism prophylaxis protocol.
Outcomes
Outcomes

Outcomes
Outcomes largely are related to the degree of residual deformity that results in FAI. Mild
deformity may be managed via arthroscopy. Moderate deformity often is better
managed via open procedures, such as a mini-open anterior approach or surgical hip
dislocation. Moderate-to-severe SCFE may be managed via a combination of surgical hip
dislocation and flexion-internal rotation intertrochanteric osteotomy with substantial
improvements in multiple outcome scores (Resource 9). 
Ultimately, osteoarthritis is a common final pathway for patients with SCFE. A minimum
of 2% of patients with SCFE will undergo total hip arthroplasty (THA), with studies
reporting a THA incidence as high as 28%, which is considerably higher than that for the
average population (approximately 1% to 2%). In addition, THA occurs at a considerably
younger age, resulting in substantial restrictions, increased wear and need for earlier
and more revisions, and a risk for THA complications. In combination with osteonecrosis
and subsequent surgery for symptomatic FAI, the overall rate of additional surgical
management because of the natural history of in situ epiphysiodesis of SCFE is almost
32% to 33%.2
